newsitem.title: UK: Horlick seeks settlement with Morgan Grenfell.
newsitem.headline: Horlick seeks settlement with Morgan Grenfell.

text.p: Former Morgan Grenfell fund manager Nicola Horlick, dubbed "superwoman" by the British press, wants an amicable settlement with her ex-employer following her high profile resignation last week, her lawyer said on Monday.
But Horlick, a 35-year-old mother-of-five and one of the most prominent fund managers in London, is prepared to sue if they cannot strike a deal.

"She is still hopeful that there might be an amicable resolution. If she is not able to get a quick and amicable resolution then she is still looking at legal action on the grounds that she was constructively dismissed," said John Farr, a partner at law firm Herbert Smith which represents Horlick.
Farr told reporters at the firm's London offices that Horlick's first priority was to get her job back as head of British pension fund business at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management(MGAM).

Farr said that if Horlick did not get her job back then she wanted compensation. He added Horlick wanted the matter resolved as quickly as possible, adding he hoped this could be "within the week or the next few days".
She was suspended by MGAM last Tuesday for an alleged breach of contract just days after being promoted to managing director by chief executive Robert Smith.

MGAM is owned by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's powerful Deutsche Bank. It has some 70 billion pounds ($116.3 billion) worth of funds under management of which 18 billion pounds is under its UK pension fund business.
It has struggled to restore its reputation since last year's revelations of irregularities at three of its retail investment funds which led to the sacking of fund manager Peter Young.
Young, who denies any involvement in criminal activity, is now under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO).
Horlick's departure has rattled some MGAM pension fund clients who have voiced concern over the stability of the management team.

No fund has withdrawn its business as a result of Horlick's departure although several have said they are reviewing their options. MGAM has carried out an intensive lobbying campaign to reassure clients about the loyalty of key personnel.

Smith suspended Horlick alleging that she had been in discussions about joining a rival bank along with members of her team and the plot thickened over the weekend as it emerged that Horlick had tentatively discussed plans for a management buyout of DMG's UK pension fund business.
Horlick has strenously denied allegations that she was about to move with her team to a rival firm, widely rumoured to have been Dutch bank ABN AMRO.
However she admitted this weekend she did meet a friend from ABN AMRO in December at what she insists was a personal lunch.

MGAM declined to comment on the latest developments except to reiterate the position it took last Friday, when it said it had no plans for any action of its own as Horlick was no longer one of its employees.

Horlick's battle with MGAM has been played out in the public domain, as accompanied by a posse of reporters and photographers, she first stormed the firm's London offices on Friday where she failed to see bosses then made a whirlwind visit to Deutsche's Frankfurt headquarters where she met representatives of the German bank.
Horlick's lawyer Farr said she had been promised by Deutsche Bank "that the matter would be looked into."
Farr said newspaper reports that Horlick was talking to MGAM clients about a move to another firm were "totally untrue".
On the doorstep of her Kensington home in west London on Monday morning Horlick said: "This is not about money - this is about clearing my name."
Asked about her aim, she said she still wanted her job back but added: "As the days go by, that may be becoming a little unrealistic."
